nodes.label: Client
nodes.summary: Calls get(key) and put(key, context, object). The context carries the vector-clock version it read.
nodes.details: Paper §4.1: get returns one object or a list of conflicting versions plus a context. Keys and objects are opaque byte arrays; an MD5 hash of the key picks the ring position.

nodes.label: Coordinator node
nodes.summary: Any of the top-N nodes in the key's preference list. Runs a per-request state machine, writes locally, fans out to replicas, waits for W (or R) replies.
nodes.details: Paper §4.5, §5: the write coordinator is chosen as the node that replied fastest to the previous read, to avoid overloading the first node and improve 99.9th-percentile latency.

nodes.label: Replica 2 (successor)
nodes.summary: Second of the N=3 owners: next clockwise node on the ring.
nodes.details: N−1 clockwise successors, skipping positions so every replica is a distinct physical node (§4.3).

nodes.label: Replica down (A)
nodes.summary: An owner that is temporarily unreachable.
nodes.details: With a sloppy quorum, its replica goes to the next healthy node instead (§4.6).

nodes.label: Stand-in node + hint store
nodes.summary: Next healthy node on the ring holds the replica with a hint naming the intended owner, in a separate local database scanned periodically, and hands it back on recovery.
nodes.details: §4.6 hinted handoff. Works best when churn is low. If the stand-in disappears first, anti-entropy has to repair.

nodes.label: Vector clocks
nodes.summary: (node, counter) pairs per version. Detect ancestors (discardable) versus concurrent versions (both kept for reconciliation).
nodes.details: §4.4. Truncated when the clock exceeds a threshold ("say 10") by dropping the oldest pair. Cassandra instead uses per-mutation timestamps and last-write-wins (Cassandra docs).

nodes.label: Merkle-tree anti-entropy
nodes.summary: Per-key-range hash trees compared between replicas to find and fix lasting divergence with little data transfer.
nodes.details: Paper §4.7. Cassandra also uses Merkle trees and adds sub-range and incremental repair.

nodes.label: Gossip membership
nodes.summary: Each node contacts a random peer every second and reconciles membership history and token ownership, so every node can route a key directly (zero-hop). Seeds prevent logical partitions.
nodes.details: Paper §4.8. Failure detection is local to each node. Cassandra: Phi Accrual detector on every node.

nodes.label: Local storage engine
nodes.summary: Pluggable per node: Berkeley DB (most production instances), BDB Java Edition, MySQL, or an in-memory buffer with a persistent backing store.

steps.caption: The client sends put(key, context, object). Any node can receive it, and routes it to a coordinator among the key's top N owners without extra hops.
Routing works because gossip has already told every node which tokens its peers own (zero-hop).
The coordinator builds the new version's vector clock from the context the client supplied.
It writes the new version to its own storage engine.
It sends the version and clock to the other N−1 replicas.
With (N,R,W)=(3,2,2), success needs W−1 more acks. It can reply as soon as one replica answers.
The coordinator acknowledges. The slowest replica may still be catching up (eventual consistency).
A put arrives while one owner (A) is unreachable.
Sloppy quorum: the replica goes to the next healthy node on the ring, tagged with a hint that it belongs to A.
The write still meets W, so the client gets success.
When A recovers, the stand-in node delivers the hinted replica and can then delete its copy.
Replicas build a Merkle tree for each key range they share.
Two replicas exchange tree roots and descend only into branches whose hashes differ, then copy just the out-of-sync keys.
